question: According to the Regulatory Scrutiny Board’s Annual Report 2025, in 2025 the Commission adopted a total of 116 legislative proposals and 741 delegated and implementing acts. Only 38 legislative proposals had an impact assessment.

The Regulatory Scrutiny Board itself, an internal and independent body of the Commission, did not give a single positive opinion among the 25 impact assessments it analysed at first instance, recording a negative opinion rate of 56 % and classifying the average quality of the reports as ‘weak’ or ‘unsatisfactory’. The Board also found that many impact assessments lacked adequate quantification of costs and benefits.

This situation shows that the European Union legislates extensively, poorly and without taking into account the socio-economic realities or the views of its own quality control body. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission believe that regulating massively benefits companies, families and workers?
Is the Commission aware that its over-regulation is leading to a transfer of income from the productive economy to the compliance industry?
Does the Commission agree that failing to carry out impact assessments shows that it is driven by its own political agenda and interests, and not by the problems facing Europeans?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Competitiveness and making business easier and faster in Europe are key priorities for this Commission.

Its better regulation and regulatory tools (impact assessments, evaluations and stakeholders’ engagement) support designing evidence-based policies and laws that achieve their objectives in the most effective and efficient way, responsive to the needs of EU citizens, businesses, and civil society. Impact assessments provide evidence-based answers to key questions regarding the expected impact of a new initiative.

They include an estimation of benefits and quantification of costs, including all compliance costs where this is feasible and proportionate. The Commission proposes laws and regulations where the benefits outweigh the associated costs. The Better Regulation Guidelines1 set several criteria to determine when an initiative needs an impact assessment.

The main ones are that there must be a political choice and significant impacts to consider. Further to the Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’2 more initiatives are to be accompanied by an impact assessment, including targeted or urgent initiatives, where feasible. Cases of exceptional urgency may require derogations.

Moreover, several legislative proposals could be accompanied by one single impact assessment. The Commission is pursuing ambitious simplification to lighten the EU regulatory burden, while maintaining high regulatory standards. Burden reduction targets (to lower the administrative burden by at least 25% for all businesses and by at least 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises) contribute to this ambition.
To create a more cohesive and efficient single market, the Commission will ensure that new legislative proposals avoid regulatory complexity and fragmentation.
